column1: What is the single invariant that determines pitch and tone color in an organ pipe?
column2: The pipe's length and whether the top is open or stopped — length sets fundamental pitch, and open vs. stopped determines which harmonics are present.

column1: How does an open pipe's fundamental frequency relate to its length?
column2: f ≈ v / (2L), where v ≈ 343 m/s — the fundamental equals speed of sound divided by twice the pipe length.

column1: Why does a stopped (capped) pipe sound an octave lower than an open pipe of the same physical length, and what harmonics does it produce?
column2: Capping the top forces the wave to fold back, doubling the effective length (so pitch drops an octave) and cancels even harmonics, leaving only odd harmonics (1st, 3rd, 5th) — producing the hollow Bourdon/Gedackt sound.

column1: What does the 'foot' number on an organ stop (e.g., 8', 4', 16') actually denote?
column2: The approximate physical length of the open pipe sounding the lowest note (C), which directly sets the pitch: 8' sounds as written, 4' an octave higher, 16' an octave lower.

column1: What is the governing rule for using mutation stops like 2⅔' Nazard or 1⅗' Tierce?
column2: Never draw a mutation without its octave foundation (8' + 4') already sounding — alone it sounds like a disembodied parallel pitch; with foundation it locks in as a harmonic partial of a composite tone.

column1: Why do reed pipes speak almost instantly compared to flue pipes, and what practical consequence does this have for articulation?
column2: Reed pipes vibrate a brass tongue against a shallot with no standing wave 'build-up' needed, so they speak instantly; flue pipes need a few milliseconds of 'chiff' transient. Détaché gaps that work on principal choruses can sound choppy on reeds because reeds don't need the flue's recovery time.

column1: Why is reed pipe tuning done by ear in small increments rather than by calculation?
column2: The tuning wire changes the effective tongue length in a nonlinear way, so reed tuning cannot be predicted mathematically and must be adjusted incrementally by ear.

column1: Approximately how much does pipe pitch shift per degree Celsius, and what is the practical performance implication?
column2: About 0.3 cents per °C; a cold cathedral can drift 10–15 cents over a three-hour service, so performers should avoid exposed octaves/fifths in solo passages when the room is still warming.

column1: What are the organist's only available controls for dynamics/expression, given that organ keys have no velocity sensitivity?
column2: Which stops are drawn (timbre + amplitude), Swell box expression pedal (shutter position), articulation (note duration/silence), and texture density (number of simultaneous voices/couplers).

column1: What tonal character and harmonic content define Principal (Diapason) stops, and what is the 'working rule' for building registrations?
column2: Open cylindrical metal pipes producing a nearly complete, evenly-balanced harmonic series — bright and choral. Rule: when in doubt, build registrations on 8' Principal, not 8' Flute.

column1: In Simandl-style organ terminology, what combination of stops (8'+4'+2⅔'+2'+1⅗') recreates, and why?
column2: It recreates a Baroque cornet/plenum sound — drawing these together hand-builds the harmonic series (fundamental plus 2nd, 3rd, 4th, and 5th partials) into one composite timbre, the essence of additive synthesis via stops.

column1: Why must organ shoes have thin leather soles rather than rubber soles?
column2: Leather glides smoothly on the pedal edges, allowing precise toe-to-heel movement, while rubber grabs the pedals and throws off timing.
